lead: A GIS layer is only useful if its numbers land on the right spot. Latitude and longitude describe a place on a curved earth; easting and northing describe it on a flat grid. A projection converts one to the other, and a datum says which earth the numbers belong to. Every layer must state its datum, projection and units, or features from different sources will not line up. District GIS, cadastral maps and utility networks all depend on this.
prereq: You need: datums and coordinate systems from the foundations of surveying, and how coordinates ride with the geometry in raster and vector models.

blocks.text: A position on the earth is a latitude (angle north or south of the equator) and a longitude (angle east or west of the prime meridian), both in degrees measured on an ellipsoid, a smooth mathematical surface close to the real earth. The geoid is a different surface: mean sea level, continued under the land. A datum fixes one chosen ellipsoid to the earth with a stated origin and orientation, so a coordinate names one place and no other. WGS84 is the global datum of GNSS. Older Indian topographic sheets use the Everest ellipsoid fixed by an older Indian datum; the newer open series maps use WGS84.

Degrees do not give flat-plane distance. One degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator and shrinks to zero at the poles, so geometry in degrees is distorted. A projection turns latitude and longitude into easting and northing in metres on a plane. No projection keeps every property: it can keep shape (conformal), keep area (equal-area), keep one distance, or keep directions from one point. Pick by the job.

sections.h3: Projection families and the UTM grid

blocks.text: Cylindrical projections wrap a cylinder around the earth; conic projections use a cone; azimuthal projections use a plane touching at one point. Transverse Mercator is a cylinder turned sideways, touching along a meridian, so it suits a north-south strip of country.

UTM divides the world into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, numbered from zone 1 at 180° W. Zone n runs from 180° + 6(n − 1) to 180° + 6n degrees. So zone number = floor((longitude + 180) ÷ 6) + 1. Each zone has a central meridian. There the scale factor is 0.9996: a 1000 m distance on the ellipsoid measures 999.6 m on the grid, 0.4 m short per kilometre. About 180 km either side the factor is 1, and further out it exceeds 1. A distance measured on the ground is first reduced to the ellipsoid (multiply by R ÷ (R + h) for a site h metres up) and then multiplied by the scale factor. A false easting of 500 000 m is added so eastings never go negative; a false northing of 10 000 000 m does the same for northings in the southern hemisphere. India falls roughly in zones 42 to 47.

Software reprojects on the fly, converting a layer into the display projection. That fixes the projection only. A wrong datum still shifts features, by a hundred metres or more between WGS84 and an old Indian datum. Every sheet's margin names its datum and projection, so read the margin rather than assume.

A dashed central meridian at 81 degrees east is labelled scale factor 0.9996 and easting 500 000 metres; two dotted lines about 180 kilometres either side mark scale factor 1. A point at 80 degrees east, 13 degrees north is joined to the central meridian by a double arrow labelled about 108 kilometres.

examples.question: A point near Chennai is at 80° E, 13° N. Find (a) its UTM zone number, (b) the zone's central meridian, (c) how far west of that meridian the point lies, and (d) the grid length of a 1000 m line measured on the ground at 100 m above the ellipsoid near the central meridian. Take R = 6 378 000 m.
steps: (b) Zone 44 runs from −180 + 6 × 43 = 78° E to 84° E. Its central meridian is 78° + 3° = 81° E.
(c) The point is 81° − 80° = 1° west of it. On the ground that is about 111.3 km × cos 13° = 111.3 × 0.974 = 108.4 km, so its easting is roughly 500 000 − 0.9996 × 108 400 ≈ 391 600 m.
(d) Reduce to the ellipsoid: 1000 × 6 378 000 ÷ (6 378 000 + 100) = 999.984 m. Apply the scale factor: 999.984 × 0.9996 = 999.584 m.
Check: the scale factor alone gives 999.600 m; the 100 m height takes off another 0.016 m. The false easting keeps every easting in the zone positive.
examples.answer: Zone 44, central meridian 81° E, point about 1° (108 km) west of it with easting near 391 600 m; the 1000 m ground line becomes 999.584 m on the grid.
examples.check:
import math
lon = 80.0
zone = math.floor((lon + 180) / 6) + 1
west = -180 + 6 * (zone - 1)
cm = west + 3
grid = 1000 * 0.9996
diff = 1000 - grid
print(int(zone))
print(int(cm))
print(round(grid, 1))
print(round(diff, 1))

traps: Feeding degrees into software that expects metres, or the reverse.
Assuming two layers with the same numeric range share a datum; equal numbers are not equal places.
Believing on-the-fly reprojection repairs a wrong datum. It repairs the projection only.
Choosing a projection before deciding which property (area, shape or distance) the job needs.
Forgetting the false easting and northing. Without them, points west of the central meridian get negative eastings and southern-hemisphere points get negative northings.
Applying 0.9996 straight to a taped ground distance. Reduce it to the ellipsoid first, then apply the scale factor.

quiz.q: Define a datum in one line.
quiz.a: An ellipsoid fixed to the earth with a stated origin and orientation, so coordinates refer to one place.

quiz.q: Why can a GIS not measure distance directly in degrees?
quiz.a: A degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator and falls to zero at the poles, so degree geometry is not a plane distance.

quiz.q: Find the UTM zone of a point at 77° E.
A 5000 m distance, already reduced to the ellipsoid, lies on the central meridian of a UTM zone. What is its grid length?
Two layers share a projection, but features in one sit about 200 m off the other. Diagnosis?
quiz.a: A datum mismatch, for example WGS84 coordinates loaded into a layer built on the Everest-based Indian datum. Reprojection will not remove it; transform the datum with the right parameters.

quiz.q: Why is a false easting of 500 000 m added in UTM?
quiz.a: So that eastings inside the 6° zone stay positive and the grid carries no negative signs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every projection and datum pair is registered by a numeric EPSG code; WGS84 with UTM zone 44N is EPSG:32644, which is why GIS files store a code rather than a name. Survey departments are moving to datum epochs, because plate motion shifts WGS84 coordinates by centimetres every year. Search 'EPSG registry' and 'datum epoch' next.
